messages.subject_clean: Regarding the difference between model$summary.fitted.values and model$summary.random
messages.body_plain:
Hello- I have been working through several books on disease mapping and have run into something I am not at all clear on. I am hoping the group can help clear this up for me.
In Blangiardo and Cameletti, Spatial and Spatiotemporal  Bayesian Models in R-INLA, they utilize the familiar London suicide dataset to calculate "borough-specific" relative risks by exponentiating the area specific residuals from the first n rows (S+U) from the $summary.random$id returns. In Morgana, Geospatial Health Data, Modelling and Visualization with R-INLA and Shiny, relative risk is calculated by $summary.fitted.values.  Now clearly these values do not match in my models and I don't think I would expect them to. So I am a little unclear on what the difference between these two relative risks are and what that specifically means. Is one just for the random effects and the other for random and fixed effects? I have looked through the discussion board for the answer and it is likely the answer is right in front of me and I am not seeing it.

Many thanks,

Dan J.

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Regarding the difference between model$summary.fitted.values and model$summary.random
messages.body_plain:
I think this is what you ask for.

if you have a random variable x, and y=exp(x),

then

	E(y) !=  exp(E(x))

but the quantiles of 'y' will be exp of the quantiles of 'x'.

so the quantiles will be correct but the mean will be a little off.

this is the B&C approach.

for Moraga, then the density for the fitted values are computed as
y=exp(x), from the density of 'x',  using a change of variable formula,
hence for the fitted values then E() and Var() will also be correct.

Best
H

One way to approximate it is to make predictions at a fine grid of points and then take their mean. So I think I want to add a lincomb to inla() which is the average of the fitted values but I only see examples of linear combinations of parameters, not fitted values.. How can I do this? Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SPDE predict spatial mean
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

You'd need to construct the vector(s) of weights needed to construct the needed linear combination of latent variables.
Some of this can be done with the help of the ipoints() function in the inlabru package (github.com/fbachl/inlabru <http://github.com/fbachl/inlabru> for the latest version, and inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> for somewhat outdated tutorials) that has support of things like this. If you do the whole estimation via the inlabru interface you can also use the inlabru predict() method to compute what you're looking for via posterior simulations (this moves all the inla.stack stuff away from your code, as it's automatically handled inside inlabru)

The following takes a SpatialPolygons object that you wish to integrate over, and (by default) calculates the integration weights points on the mesh needed to evaluate the integral over the polygon. If the mesh is the same as your spde mesh, then the integration points will be the subset of the mesh points with positive integration weight.:
  ips <- ipoints(integration_polygon, mesh)

If the estimation is done in inlabru, you can then do
  predict(fit, ips, ~ sum(weight * your_predictor_expression))
to compute the prediction of the integral (divide the weights by the polygon area to get the average instead of the integral).

To instead use this to build a lincomb for inla, more steps are involved that I don't recall the details of, but from what I recall
  A.integrate = inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = ips, weights = ips$weight / totalarea, block = 1, block.rescale = "weights")
would construct the 1-row linear combination matrix to compute the average across a field, but I think you need to express the lincomb in the latent variables and not the fitted values.

If your fitted values involve a nonlinear link function, then the inlabru predict method is easier, as you can include that in the expression, but lincomb can only be linear in the latent variables.

A hybrid option is to mimic the inlabru::predict() method directly in inla by inla.posterior.sample and inla.posterior.sample.eval, that does a similar thing as inlabru::generate() & predict().

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SPDE predict spatial mean
messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric,
I assume you’re using the latest github version of inlabru? (The CRAN version will soon be replaced by a new version from github)

You can call generate() instead of predict() to get the samples, and compute other summaries than those predict() gives you.

When given a region and a mesh, by default inlabru will first generate an integration scheme within each triangle, then remove points outside the given region, and finally aggregate the integration scheme onto the mesh nodes. For integrals that are linear on the triangles, this is exact.
When the region boundary crosses the interior of a triangle, this will lead to some integration weight on the vertices just outside the region. This is normal and correct.
The aggregation step can be disabled by setting
options=list(bru_int_args=list(method=“direct”))
The default is method=“stable”.

When no mesh is given, it produces a warning, and builds a mesh internally to construct the integration scheme on. However, it doesn’t have information about suitable mesh generation parameters, so it’s better to supply your own mesh, where you can control the resolution; normally the mesh used to build the SPDE model is appropriate.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric,

when fitting an lgcp model, one needs to ensure that the integration points are placed so that the likelihood approximation is stable (which is achieved by having integration points at the mesh vertices, but other more involved options are possible).
When just computing integrals, regardless of what the model likelihood was, there is more freedom in how the integration is done, and yes,
ipoints(integration_polygon, domain=mesh, int.args=...) can be used to construct such an integration scheme, either per-vertex (int.args=list(method="stable")) or points within-triangle (int.args=list(method="direct", nsub2 = ...)).

In any case, having many more integration points than the mesh doesn't really make a difference, since the variability of the field is limited by the triangles themselves, but
if integrating a nonlinear function of the field, the density of integration points within a triangle does matter a bit, and then the "direct" method is appropriate.

The correlation range does give some indication of how nonlinear the function might be within a triangle (and possibly if even fewer points than the mesh points are needed), but when it's just a post-processing step from generated samples, it's likely not worth the effort, as increasing the number of triangle-internal integration points quickly produces a very accurate approximation when it's needed, and is still fast when it's not needed;
In inlabru, the sampling just generates the latent variables (and hyperparameters), and the integrals approximation is computed for each generated sample; having fewer integration points does not improve the speed of the sampling step, only the simple postprocessing step, and the same should old in your MCMC case; the integral computations are no coupled to the MCMC chain.

Finn

Hi,
Possible causes depend on the details of the input data. What’s the extent of loc.mesh? E.g. summary(loc.mesh) ?
For some input geometries there may be special cases that lead to infinite loops, which I think is the likely reason in your case, since 20000 isn’t very large, and if Max.edge implies a very large output, it would be likely to run into memory issues instead of just keep working. See the help text for information on an option that can limit the maximum mesh size; that doesn’t prevent infinite loops, but does guard against accidentally large meshes.
The special geometries that cause infinite loops can usually be avoided by defining the mesh boundary with inla.nonconvex.hull instead of the plain “offset” method.

Finn

Let u be the normal iid effect with unknown precision,  then the first
model says that

	predictor = intercept + X * u

while the second model says that

	predictor = intercept + beta * X + X * u

where beta is the regression coefficient for X.

messages.subject: Question about correlated random slopes and intercepts
messages.subject_clean: Question about correlated random slopes and intercepts
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

New user, looking into INLA as a possible mixed modelling software, due to needing to work with some mixed-models with random effects with many levels. I'm trying to track down why INLA seems to be giving me a very different result than lme4 does. What I'm trying to figure out is modelling correlated random slopes and intercepts. When I use INLA, I'm currently getting a really strongly negative correlation between the random slopes and intercepts by subject, when it should be really strong positive correlation. I'm trying to figure out if I've made an error in setting up the formula, or if it's maybe something to do with the priors on random slope correlatioms in INLA.

Thanks,
Bryor

library(INLA)

### simulation params
n <- 5000
n_items <- 50
n_subjects <- 30
item_sd <- .2
b0 <- 0
b1 <- 0.5
subject_intercept_sd <- 2
subject_slope_sd <- 2
subject_intercept_slope_correlation <- .9
noise_sd <- 1
m <- matrix(c(1,subject_intercept_slope_correlation,subject_intercept_slope_correlation,1),nrow = 2)
slope_cov_mat <- diag(c(subject_intercept_sd, subject_slope_sd)) %*% m %*% diag(c(subject_intercept_sd, subject_slope_sd))

### random variables
x <- rnorm(n)
subjects <- sample(rep(1:n_subjects, length.out = n), replace = T)
items <- sample(rep(1:n_items, length.out = n), replace = T)
item_random_intercepts <- rnorm(n_items, item_sd)
subject_random_effects <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_subjects, mu = c(0,0), Sigma = slope_cov_mat)

y <- b0 +
  (b1 + subject_random_effects[subjects,2]) * x +
  item_random_intercepts[items] +
  subject_random_effects[subjects,1] +
  rnorm(n, sd = noise_sd)

dat <- data.frame(y, x, subjects, items)

dat$i <- dat$subjects
dat$j <- dat$i + dat$subjects

summary(mod_inla <- inla(y ~ x + f(items, model="iid") + f(j, x, copy = "i") + f(i, model="iid2d",n=2*n),data=dat,control.compute=list(config = TRUE)))
### very strong negative correlation

library(lme4)

summary(mod_lme4 <- lmer(y ~ x + (1|items) + (1+x|subjects), data=dat))
### returns close to true correlation

Hi INLA Groups,

I hope you have spent a happy Christmas.
I want to specifiy an interaction of space and time components by analogy the IV interaction from Held.
The spatial random effect (u) reads,  u \sim MVN \left ( 0, \sigma_{u}^{2}(I-W)(I-{W}') \right )
I is an identity matrix and W is a spatia adjacent matrix, and there is not spatial strength coefficent in the covariance matrix.

The temporal random effects (t) follows a first-order autoregressive process.

In this context, I would like to know, whether we can specifiy an interaction between u and t following the specification of IV interaction?

I try the following code:

library("DClusterm")
data(brainNM)
library(INLA)

nm.adj <- poly2nb(brainst@sp)
adj.mat <- as(nb2mat(nm.adj, style = "B"), "Matrix")

brainst @ data$ID3<- as.numeric(brainst @ data$ID)
brainst @ data$ID.Year <- brainst @ data$Year - 1973 + 1

Q_sar<- (Diagonal(nrow(adj.mat), x = 1) - adj.mat) %*% t(Diagonal(nrow(adj.mat), x = 1) - adj.mat)

brain.st4.sar1 <- inla(Observed ~ 1 +
                        f(ID3, model = "generic0", Cmatrix = Q_sar,
                          group = ID.Year, control.group = list(model = "ar1")
                          ),
                      data = brainst@data, E = Expected, verbose = T, family = "poisson",
                      control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1))
summary(brain.st4.sar1)

If the code is correct, how to specifiy prior for this interaction term?

Thanks in advance.
All the best,
Charles

Hi Leo,

technically speaking, the stochastic PDE models of order 2 are closely related to discrete domain simultaneous auto-regression (SAR) models of the type you describe. These SPDE models have discretised precisions with the same structure as the discrete SAR models, so inla.spde2.generic() could in principle be used to construct more general versions (that could include a dependence strength parameter). However, in your special case where there is only a global precision scaling parameter, the generic0 approach that is in your code is the most efficient solution.

The code looks fine, except that, if I understand correctly, your I-W matrix has row-sum zero, Is your precision (I-W)(I-W)' or (I-W)'(I-W) ?
For example, if the purely spatial model is invariant to adding a constant, then the kronecker product model will be invariant to adding a different constant to each time step.
Using rank-deficient models as building blocks can be a pain, as you need to keep track of the rank-deficiencies, and because introducing constraints changes the model interpretation and behaviour;
for example, imposing a sum-to-zero constraint on each time step means the one will likely need to add a separate time-process to the model to allow it to vary usefully across time.
Alternatively, if invariance to adding a different global constant across space for each time point is what you want, then you can leave the g=kronecker model as it is, and instead remove the global intercept from the model, since otherwise it will be non-identifiable.

Finn

> > > technically speaking, the stochastic PDE models of order 2 are closely related to discrete domain simultaneous auto-regression (SAR) models of the type you describe. These SPDE models have discretised precisions with the same structure as the discrete SAR models, so inla.spde2.generic() could in principle be used to construct more general versions (that could include a dependence strength parameter). However, in your special case where there is only a global precision scaling parameter, the generic0 approach that is in your code is the most efficient solution.
> > >
> > > The code looks fine, except that, if I understand correctly, your I-W matrix has row-sum zero, Is your precision (I-W)(I-W)' or (I-W)'(I-W) ?
> > > For example, if the purely spatial model is invariant to adding a constant, then the kronecker product model will be invariant to adding a different constant to each time step.
> > > Using rank-deficient models as building blocks can be a pain, as you need to keep track of the rank-deficiencies, and because introducing constraints changes the model interpretation and behaviour;
> > > for example, imposing a sum-to-zero constraint on each time step means the one will likely need to add a separate time-process to the model to allow it to vary usefully across time.
> > > Alternatively, if invariance to adding a different global constant across space for each time point is what you want, then you can leave the g=kronecker model as it is, and instead remove the global intercept from the model, since otherwise it will be non-identifiable.
